coherence.reasons: Both lead with the same answer and support it with four parallel arguments (market, unit economics, cash, software alternative) that the body pages prove in order. X's summary is tighter and every title is a claim. Y adds an explicit frame of four 'what would have to be true' tests, and each test maps to a section, an option-table criterion and a reopening trigger, which makes the hierarchy slightly more closed-loop. Against that, Y has one internal inconsistency: page 10 shows −$4.7M at month 18 on the second reading of the $9.5M, while the appendix shows −$2.5M and 'runs out ≈M15' from a different burn model. X's cash figures are consistent throughout (month 13, −$4.7M). Net, Y's test-to-trigger structure edges it, but only just.

judgment.reasons: Both reach the key's preferred recommendation (do not launch; fund software; sell fast delivery to grocers) and both reject the own-store pilot rather than drifting into 'launch one city to prove density'. Y weighs the alternatives more fully. It costs the one-store pilot bottom-up (≈$3.4M) and shows it breaches the runway floor by month 6, and it notes the learning is mostly already visible from the 14 software sites. It adds a status-quo option, compares reversibility, and stress-tests its own recommendation (floor holds down to ≈34% growth or costs +10% a year). It also tranches the hires against bookings and adds a funding trigger (software at break-even or ring-fenced capital) that stops the operator plan returning by stealth. X's option table is sound but thinner: the pilot is rated 'partly fits cash' without a runway test, and one of its four criteria (channel conflict) rests on an inference X itself calls untested. X's idea of testing a service fee at a customer site is a good capital-light learning route; Y has an equivalent in its paid grocer pilots and benchmark-site triggers.

evidence.reasons: Both reproduce every required figure correctly: −$6.17 median, −$1.76 best observed, −$12.57 pop-up, 41.5% CAGR, $2.5M left against a $4.8M floor, and −$1.05 for the Zipcart fix at median with the 14% volume loss. I checked the secondary arithmetic in both (bridges, single-input reversions, payback months, sensitivity grid, break-even volumes) and it holds. X adds useful single-input break-evens (AOV $63, 14.4 orders per rider-hour, volume cannot fix a negative variable margin) and a two-way sensitivity grid, and its cash arithmetic is clean. Its claim that 'pricing, not density, did the work' at Zipcart slightly overreaches, since the result came in Zipcart's densest city, but X does show the fix gives about +$3.97 at best observed inputs. Y uses the critical evidence a little more inventively: the break-even density under Zipcart's fix (1,042–1,211 orders a day), the point that the benchmark median already includes whatever Parcelbird's software adds, and a caveated sizing of ≈$27M implied acquisition spend against a $9.5M budget. But Y carries a numerical inconsistency on the second cash reading (month 15 and −$2.5M in the appendix against −$4.7M on page 10; flat burn gives month 13). Y's richer inferences and X's cleaner numbers roughly offset.

revision.reasons: Both correctly reject the founders' hypothesis while crediting what is true in it: growth above 40% is real, the pop-up was a short temporary test, and Zipcart's positive city is engaged with rather than ignored or taken as proof. Y handles the hypothesis more explicitly. It states the founders' view, breaks it into four conditions that would have to hold, gives graded verdicts ('half met' on market, 'not met' on the others) and says plainly that the answer was changed. It also lists 'founders are right about density' as a risk with the forgone upside quantified, and maps reopening triggers to each failed test. X does the same substantively (it rebuts 'we run them better' and 'nobody owns the Midwest', and sets reopening evidence) but less systematically. Both avoid over- or under-correcting.

overall.reasons: Both are strong, defensible board papers that meet every criterion in the key: realistic unit economics, growth separated from profit, the runway check, the software alternative, and proper handling of the Zipcart evidence. X is more concise and numerically cleaner, with good break-even and sensitivity analysis. Y would serve the board somewhat better because it answers the questions an investor would ask next. It shows a one-store pilot breaches the runway floor too, shows how robust the software path is to slower growth or rising costs, makes the hires tranche-able, and sets a funding condition before the operator idea can return. It also explains why the 'we run stores better' claim is already priced into the benchmark. Y's one cash-model inconsistency on the alternative reading of the $9.5M does not affect the conclusion.
